questions.stem: Why is the defeat of the Prairial rising in May 1795 seen as a turning point?
options: It led directly to the restoration of the Bourbon monarchy
It ended the sans-culottes as an independent political force
It allowed the Jacobins to return to power in the Convention
It forced the Convention to restore the General Maximum
questions.explanation: The army disarmed the faubourgs and leading militants were arrested, so the popular movement that had driven events since 1789 was broken. Power stayed with the moderate Thermidorians; the Maximum was not restored and the monarchy did not return.

questions.stem: In 1794-95 bands of well-off young men in Paris, the 'jeunesse dorée' (gilded youth), were known for:
options: joining the royalist rebels of the Vendée as volunteer officers
guarding the Convention against the army on behalf of Robespierre
attacking Jacobins and sans-culottes and helping close the Jacobin Club
leading the sans-culottes in demands for the Constitution of 1793
questions.explanation: Encouraged by Thermidorian leaders such as Fréron, these youths beat up known Jacobins and took part in the attack that preceded the closing of the Jacobin Club in November 1794. They symbolised the shift of the streets of Paris from the radicals to the reaction.

questions.stem: In June and July 1795 an army of émigrés landed at Quiberon in Brittany with British help. What happened?
options: The British fleet withdrew before landing, and the émigrés surrendered without fighting
Republican troops under Hoche defeated them, and hundreds of captured émigrés were shot
They joined the Vendée rebels and captured Nantes, forcing the Convention to negotiate
They marched on Paris and were stopped only by the rising of 13 Vendémiaire
questions.explanation: General Hoche trapped and defeated the landing force. Several hundred émigrés taken in arms were executed under the laws against émigrés, a blow to royalist hopes of restoring the monarchy by force.

questions.stem: Under the Constitution of the Year III (1795), legislative power was held by:
options: a single National Assembly elected by all adult men
the Legislative Body and the Tribunate under a First Consul
the Senate and a Chamber of Deputies chosen by the king
the Council of Five Hundred and the Council of Ancients
questions.explanation: The Five Hundred proposed laws and the Council of Ancients (250 members aged at least 40) approved or rejected them. The Tribunate and First Consul belong to Bonaparte's Constitution of the Year VIII, after 1799.

questions.stem: How was the membership of the five-man Directory renewed under the Constitution of the Year III?
options: all five Directors were re-elected each year by every adult male citizen
the Directors served for life unless removed by the Council of Five Hundred
the senior general of the army appointed the Directors every three years
one Director left each year, chosen by lot, and the councils chose a replacement
questions.explanation: The Ancients chose each new Director from a list drawn up by the Five Hundred, and one Director left each year. The design was meant to prevent any person from dominating, as Robespierre was believed to have done through the Committee of Public Safety.

questions.stem: The Constitution of the Year III gave the Directors no power to veto laws or dissolve the councils, and a third of the councils was re-elected every year. Historians often argue this design:
options: left no legal way to break deadlock, encouraging coups against election results
gave the Directors so much power that the councils became powerless rubber stamps
made elections so rare that public opinion could not influence the government
allowed the sans-culottes to dominate the councils through annual elections
questions.explanation: Annual elections kept returning royalist or Jacobin majorities that threatened the regime, and the Directors could not lawfully dissolve hostile councils. The result was a series of coups in 1797, 1798 and 1799, each overturning the voters' choice.

questions.stem: The 'Two-Thirds Decree' of August 1795 required that:
options: two-thirds of the Directors be former members of the Jacobin Club
two-thirds of church land be sold to pay off the national debt
two-thirds of the new councils' members come from the Convention
two-thirds of male citizens pay direct tax before they could vote
questions.explanation: The Thermidorians feared that free elections would return a royalist majority, so they guaranteed their own places in the new legislature. Anger at the decree helped spark the royalist-led rising of Vendémiaire in October 1795.

questions.stem: How did the franchise of 1795 differ from that of the Constitution of 1793?
options: Only former nobles and clergy were allowed to stand for the councils
Property qualifications returned, limiting who could act as electors
Women were allowed to vote for the first time in national elections
All adult men voted directly for the Directors and the councils
questions.explanation: The Constitution of 1793, never put into effect, promised manhood suffrage. In 1795 voters chose electors who had to meet a substantial property qualification, so power rested with men of property; women still had no vote.

questions.stem: On 13 Vendémiaire Year IV (5 October 1795) a rising of royalist-led Paris sections against the Convention was put down by troops under Barras, with Napoleon Bonaparte directing the artillery. Its main result for Bonaparte was that:
options: he was arrested and briefly imprisoned for firing on the people of Paris
he was elected one of the first five Directors under the new constitution of 1795
it ended his career in the army until he returned from Egypt in 1799
it brought him favour with the new regime and soon command of the Army of Italy
questions.explanation: Bonaparte's cannon fire cleared the streets and saved the Convention. Barras became a Director and early in 1796 Bonaparte was given command of the Army of Italy, the start of his rise.

questions.stem: Gracchus Babeuf, executed in 1797 after his 'Conspiracy of the Equals' was betrayed, is often seen as a forerunner of communism because he:
options: was the first revolutionary to call for the execution of the king and the nobles
argued that true equality required abolishing private property, not just equal rights
led the first successful workers' government in Paris, which lasted for two years
wrote the Constitution of the Year III and its declaration of citizens' duties
questions.explanation: Babeuf, writing in his paper the Tribune of the People, went beyond the legal equality of 1789 to demand common ownership. His plot to overthrow the Directory failed, but later socialists, influenced by his follower Buonarroti's account of the plot, saw him as a pioneer.

questions.stem: In the elections of 1797 royalists and moderates won a majority of the seats being contested. The coup of 18 Fructidor Year V (4 September 1797) responded by:
options: restoring Louis XVIII as constitutional monarch under the Constitution of 1791
cancelling all future elections and returning power to the Committee of Public Safety
annulling elections in many departments and deporting leading deputies, with army support
dissolving the Directory and handing executive power to Bonaparte as First Consul
questions.explanation: Three Directors, backed by troops under Augereau sent by Bonaparte, purged the councils: elections were annulled in 49 departments and leading royalists were deported to Guiana. The Director Carnot fled. It showed the regime depended on the army to survive.

questions.stem: In the coup of Fructidor (1797) the Directory acted against royalists; in Floréal (1798) it annulled the election of many left-wing deputies. What do the two coups together suggest about the Directory?
options: It was controlled by royalists who used the coups to destroy the republic
It respected election results except when the army threatened mutiny
It aimed to hold a moderate centre by overriding voters on either side
It shifted steadily left, moving from royalism towards Jacobin democracy
questions.explanation: The Directors saw both a royal restoration and a return of Jacobin rule as threats, so they struck at whichever side the voters favoured. The policy is sometimes called the 'see-saw' and it eroded the regime's legitimacy.

questions.stem: In the 'coup' of 30 Prairial Year VII (June 1799):
options: Bonaparte seized power with troops and dissolved the councils
the Directors arrested Babeuf and closed the Jacobin clubs of Paris
royalists captured the Tuileries and proclaimed Louis XVIII king
the councils forced out several Directors, strengthening Sieyès
questions.explanation: This time the legislature turned on the executive, blaming the Directors for military defeats. Sieyès, who had joined the Directory in May 1799, emerged stronger and began to look for a general to help him revise the constitution.

questions.stem: Which measure of 1799 revived fears of a return to the Terror?
options: The Law of Hostages, allowing relatives of émigrés and rebels to be held
The Concordat with the Pope, restoring all of the Catholic Church's lands
The Civil Code, making all male citizens equal before the law
The abolition of conscription and the return of a volunteer army
questions.explanation: Facing invasion and royalist revolt, the councils passed the Law of Hostages and a forced loan on the rich in mid-1799. Property owners feared a new Jacobin emergency government, which made many welcome Brumaire. The Concordat and Civil Code came later under Bonaparte.

questions.stem: Which treaty of October 1797 ended Bonaparte's Italian campaign by making peace with Austria?
options: The Treaty of Tilsit
The Treaty of Lunéville
Treaty of Campo Formio
The Treaty of Amiens
questions.explanation: At Campo Formio Austria gave up the Austrian Netherlands (Belgium) and recognised the Cisalpine Republic, receiving Venice in return. Bonaparte negotiated it largely on his own, a sign of his growing independence. Amiens (1802), Tilsit (1807) and Lunéville (1801) came later.

questions.stem: The 'sister republics' set up by France between 1795 and 1799, such as the Batavian, Cisalpine and Helvetic republics, were:
options: states modelled on France that supplied it with money, troops and buffer zones
independent democracies that refused any French influence after their liberation
French departments whose deputies sat in the Council of Five Hundred
monarchies restored by the Second Coalition in lands taken from France
questions.explanation: These client republics in the Netherlands, northern Italy and Switzerland copied French institutions but were expected to pay war levies and support French armies. Spreading the revolution abroad was closely tied to funding the war.

questions.stem: Why did Bonaparte's campaign in Italy in 1796-97 matter so much to the Directory?
options: It ended the war with Britain and reopened French trade with the Caribbean colonies
It was a defensive campaign that kept Austrian armies out of Paris
It restored the Pope's power in Rome and won back Catholic support
It brought victories and plunder that helped fund a government short of money
questions.explanation: Victories such as Lodi, Arcole and Rivoli were followed by heavy levies on Italian states, which helped pay the army and the Directory. The government came to depend on its generals, especially Bonaparte, both for money and prestige.

questions.stem: Why did Bonaparte's expedition to Egypt in 1798 weaken France's position in Europe?
options: It used up all French troops, so the Directory had to abolish conscription
It helped bring Russia, Austria and the Ottomans into a Second Coalition against France
It forced France to give Belgium back to Austria in return for safe passage home
It led the United States to declare war on France and blockade its Atlantic ports
questions.explanation: The invasion of Ottoman Egypt and Nelson's destruction of the French fleet at Aboukir Bay encouraged a new coalition. In 1799 coalition armies drove the French out of much of Italy while Bonaparte's army was stranded in Egypt.

questions.stem: In 1799 the Second Coalition drove French armies out of much of Italy and threatened France's borders. How did this help Bonaparte take power?
options: The defeats united royalists and Jacobins behind the Directory against him
Defeats discredited the Directory, and he returned as an earlier victor
The Coalition demanded his appointment as ruler of France as a condition of peace
His army in Egypt defeated the Coalition alone, so the councils elected him
questions.explanation: Military failure, the Law of Hostages and royalist revolts made the regime look both weak and dangerous. Bonaparte's earlier victories, and the fact that he had not shared in the defeats of 1799, made him the natural ally for Sieyès's plan.

questions.stem: In 1796 the Directory replaced the collapsing assignats with a new paper currency, the mandats territoriaux. What happened to the mandats?
options: They held their value and became the basis of the franc until 1914
They were exchanged for gold at full value by the Bank of France
They were withdrawn because Bonaparte refused to accept them
They lost value rapidly and were abandoned within about a year
questions.explanation: The mandats were meant to be backed by national lands but quickly depreciated like the assignats. In 1797 France returned to metal coinage, causing deflation that hurt peasants selling produce.

questions.stem: In 1797 the finance minister Ramel wrote off about two-thirds of the state debt, a measure known as the 'bankruptcy of the two-thirds'. Its effect was to:
options: reduce the debt burden on the state while ruining many bondholders
pay all of the state's creditors in full using silver from Italy
transfer the national debt to the sister republics in Italy
end the war by giving creditors land in conquered territories
questions.explanation: Holders of government bonds lost most of their capital, but the state's interest payments fell sharply. Along with tax reforms, it gave later governments a sounder base, one reason some historians judge the Directory more favourably.

questions.stem: The Jourdan Law of September 1798 is significant because it:
options: made all young men liable to regular conscription into the army
abolished the army and replaced it with a citizens' National Guard
allowed soldiers to elect their own officers in every regiment
banned generals from holding political office in the Directory
questions.explanation: The Jourdan Law made men aged 20 to 25 liable for military service, turning the emergency levée en masse of 1793 into a permanent system. Resistance to it fed revolts, notably in Belgium, and the system later supplied Napoleon's armies.

questions.stem: On 18 Brumaire Year VIII (9 November 1799) the councils were moved from Paris to Saint-Cloud. The reason given was:
options: an outbreak of disease in Paris that made it unsafe for deputies to meet there
the approach of an Austrian army towards Paris after French defeats in Germany
a royalist rising in the capital that had seized the Tuileries palace
a supposed Jacobin plot, though the real aim was to act away from the Paris crowds
questions.explanation: Sieyès's allies in the Ancients used the claim of a conspiracy to move the legislature and give Bonaparte command of the troops. The next day, when the Five Hundred resisted, soldiers cleared the chamber and a provisional Consulate replaced the Directory.

questions.stem: When Bonaparte was jostled by deputies of the Five Hundred at Saint-Cloud on 19 Brumaire, who saved the coup by calling on the guards to clear the chamber?
options: Joseph Fouché, minister of police under the Consulate
Lucien Bonaparte, president of the Five Hundred
Paul Barras, the most powerful of the five Directors
Georges Danton, the former leader of the Indulgents
questions.explanation: Lucien, as president of the council, told the troops that deputies were threatening the general and led them in. Barras resigned during the coup, Danton had been executed in 1794, and Fouché supported the coup but did not lead the troops.

questions.stem: Under the Constitution of the Year VIII (1799), the Tribunate debated laws without voting on them, and the Legislative Body voted on laws without debating them. This arrangement:
options: gave ordinary citizens a direct vote on each law through referendums
made the Tribunate the main source of executive power in France
restored the separation of powers of the Constitution of 1791
left elected bodies weak, so real power rested with the First Consul
questions.explanation: Dividing debate from decision made the assemblies easy to control, while the First Consul proposed laws, appointed ministers and controlled foreign policy. Bonaparte, as First Consul, was the effective ruler from the start.

questions.stem: The constitution of 1799 was approved in a plebiscite announced in early 1800. Why do historians treat its result with caution?
options: Only former nobles and clergy were allowed to take part
The vote was held after Bonaparte had already been made emperor
Most departments rejected it, but the results were never published
The official 'yes' total was inflated by the government
questions.explanation: The official figure of about three million votes in favour was published, but research shows Lucien Bonaparte's interior ministry added votes, including a large block attributed to the army. Real support was much lower, though few voted against.

questions.stem: In December 1799 the consuls declared that the revolution was 'finished', having been fixed to the principles with which it began. Which evidence best supports the view that Brumaire ended the revolution rather than continued it?
options: Buyers of national lands kept the property they had bought since 1790
Careers in the army and administration remained open to men of talent
Power passed to one man, and elected bodies lost real control of government
Feudal dues abolished in 1789 to 1793 were not restored to the nobility
questions.explanation: Concentrating power in the First Consul ended the attempt to found government on elected assemblies. The other options show gains of the revolution being kept, which supports the opposing view that Bonaparte consolidated the revolution.

questions.stem: The Directory years are often associated with the 'Incroyables' and 'Merveilleuses' of Paris. They were:
options: fashionable young people whose extravagant dress mocked revolutionary austerity
radical sans-culottes who demanded price controls and the Constitution of 1793
royalist soldiers of the Vendée who fought under a white flag
deputies who refused the oath to the Constitution of the Year III
questions.explanation: Wealthy young Parisians flaunted outlandish fashions and pleasures after the Terror. They came to symbolise the reaction against Jacobin virtue and the image of the Directory as a time of corruption and luxury, though most French people lived very differently.

questions.stem: A traditional view saw the Directory as weak, corrupt and merely a bridge to Napoleon. Martyn Lyons and other historians since the 1970s have argued instead that:
options: it was more violent than the Terror, which explains its unpopularity
it made lasting reforms in finance and administration that Napoleon built on
it was a radical democracy that Napoleon destroyed to save the monarchy
it was secretly directed by Bonaparte from the time of the Vendémiaire rising
questions.explanation: Revisionists point to tax and debt reform, the work of bodies such as the National Institute and administrative changes as foundations for the Consulate. They accept its political instability but see more continuity between Directory and Consulate than the old view allowed.

questions.stem: Which reform, introduced by law in 1795 under the Thermidorian Convention and developed under the Directory, became one of the revolution's most widespread legacies?
options: The metric system of weights and measures
The revolutionary calendar of ten-day weeks
The Cult of the Supreme Being as a state religion
The election of priests and bishops by citizens
questions.explanation: The metre and gram replaced the many local measures of the old regime, and the system later spread across most of the world. The revolutionary calendar was abolished under Napoleon, and the Cult of the Supreme Being and elected clergy did not last.

questions.stem: A student argues that Brumaire was mainly the work of Bonaparte's personal ambition. Which evidence most weakens this argument?
options: Bonaparte returned from Egypt in October 1799 without any orders from the Directory
Bonaparte's troops cleared the Five Hundred from the hall at Saint-Cloud
Bonaparte became First Consul in the constitution that followed the coup
Sieyès and other politicians planned the coup and sought a general to carry it out
questions.explanation: Sieyès, a Director, wanted a stronger executive and looked for a general to support a revision of the constitution; Bonaparte was not his first choice. The other points fit the ambition argument rather than weakening it.

questions.stem: As a source on Brumaire, the official account published by the new consuls immediately afterwards is most useful as evidence of:
options: the exact words spoken by deputies inside the Orangerie at Saint-Cloud
how most French people voted in the plebiscite of early 1800
the private motives of each Director who resigned during the coup
how the plotters wanted the public to understand and justify the coup
questions.explanation: Government announcements stressed a 'Jacobin plot' and assassins' daggers to present the coup as a rescue of the republic. Such a source shows the justification offered, not a neutral record of what happened or what people privately thought.

questions.stem: Which statement best describes the relationship between the Directory and the army by 1799?
options: It relied on generals to win wars, fund the state and settle crises
Civilian control was so strong that all generals were banned from Paris
The army was loyal to the royalists and refused to defend the republic
The army had been disbanded and replaced by local National Guards
questions.explanation: Troops were used in Vendémiaire and Fructidor, conquests paid many bills and victorious generals gained prestige. By 1799 a general taking power was widely expected; the question was which one.
